title: Cyril of Jerusalem's lectures
hook: talks to the newly baptized explaining what they had just experienced

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ephrem, the deacon who set the faith to music and taught choirs to sing it. Your line was theology you can sing. Which hymn line stayed with you? Day seven hundred twenty-nine.

Jerusalem, the days after Easter. A group of people come back to church who were baptized only days ago. Before that night, they had been taught the creed and the stories, but nobody had walked them through what would actually happen to them. They went in, and it happened: words, oil, water, bread. Now they sit down, still a little dazed, and the bishop stands up. In effect he says: you've been through it. Now I'll tell you what it meant. The talks known as Cyril's lectures to the newly baptized are that explanation.
screen: `BAPTIZED A FEW DAYS AGO.` → `NOBODY EXPLAINED IT BEFOREHAND.` → `NOW, WHAT IT MEANT.`

segments.voice: These talks have a name: mystagogy. And the first thing the bishop says explains the order. He had long wanted to speak to them about these mysteries, he says, but seeing persuades more than hearing, so he waited until they had seen for themselves. First the night. Then the words. Then he walks them back through it. Remember, he says, how you stood in the outer hall, facing west, the direction of darkness, and stretched out your hand and renounced Satan. Then you turned around, to the east, toward the light. Remember how you took off your old garment, and were anointed with oil, and led to the pool, and asked whether you believed in the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Every gesture had a meaning, and now he gives it to them. Then the altar. He quotes the psalm sung at communion. In the Douay-Rheims it reads: "O taste, and see that the Lord is sweet." And he gives them a very practical instruction. When you come forward, he says, don't come with your fingers spread. Make your left hand a throne for the right, because the right hand is about to receive a King. Hollow your palm, receive the Body of Christ, and answer Amen. That's mystagogy. The Catechism of the Catholic Church uses the word for teaching that moves from the visible to the invisible, from the sign to the thing it signifies. The water, the oil, the open hand. After, the meaning.
screen: `FIRST THE NIGHT, THEN THE WORDS.` · `TURN FROM THE WEST TO THE EAST.` · `A THRONE FOR THE KING.` · `FROM THE SIGN TO WHAT IT SIGNIFIES.` · then, large: `O TASTE, AND SEE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: explain one sacrament to yourself. Settle, and breathe. Pick one you've received or watched: a baptism, communion, a wedding, an anointing. Walk through what you saw, slowly, one piece at a time. Water. Oil. A ring. Bread in an open hand. For each piece, ask: what is this pointing to? If you're not sure, just notice the question. If you're new to all this, use a ritual you've seen at a wedding or a funeral. The bell holds the time.
Mystagogy. Teaching given after the rite, leading the newly baptized from what they saw to what it means. Today's word.
Your line: after, the meaning. Today, notice one gesture you make without thinking, a sign of the cross, a handshake, a bow, and ask what it says. Day seven hundred twenty-nine.

howItsDone: In the Catholic Church the time after adult baptism at the Easter Vigil is called mystagogy: the newly baptized keep meeting during the Easter season to reflect on the sacraments they have received.

original.note: Greek: mystagogy — the name for teaching that unfolds the sacraments after they are received.

trapdoor: what you thought: mystagogy sounds like something secret and mysterious.
what it means: teaching given after baptism, walking the newly baptized back through what they had just been through.
what a scholar hears: the Catechism (1075) describes it as moving from the visible to the invisible, from the sign to the thing signified, from the sacraments to the mysteries.
